title: How To Make Classroom Management Sticky https://smartclassroommanagement.com/2010/02/20/how-to-make-classroom-management-sticky/
author: Michael Linsin
summary: Linsin opens with the story of teacher Jane Elliott's famous 1968 'blue eyes/brown eyes' exercise, drawn from the book Made To Stick, to illustrate how turning an abstract concept into a concrete experience makes a lesson memorable and lasting. He applies this insight to classroom management, arguing that traditional lecture-style teaching of rules and procedures is too abstract and 'slippery' for students to internalize. His two-step solution is experiential: first, the teacher shows students exactly what's expected through detailed, physically embodied modeling, even dressing or acting the part; second, students demonstrate the procedure back to the teacher and are tested on their understanding through direct performance rather than verbal explanation. Linsin acknowledges the approach takes more time than simply telling students what to do, but argues that's simply what good teaching requires, and points readers to further resources on experiential teaching.
points: Jane Elliott's 1968 'blue eyes/brown eyes' exercise illustrates how concrete experience makes abstract lessons memorable and lasting.
Traditional lecture-style teaching of classroom rules and procedures is too abstract for students to fully internalize.
Step one is detailed, physically embodied modeling in which the teacher shows students exactly what's expected.
Step two is having students demonstrate the procedure back to the teacher, testing understanding through actual performance.
The experiential approach takes more time than simply telling students the rules, but Linsin argues that's simply what good teaching requires.
quotes: She then explained that the brown-eyed students were smarter and superior to the blue-eyed students and therefore would be allowed extra recess.
While in the inferior group, students described feeling “sad,” “bad,” “stupid,” and “mean.” They were so affected by the negative label that even their academic performance dropped.
What Jane Elliot did was remarkable. She took something abstract to her students—discrimination—and turned it into a concrete experience.
When it comes to classroom management, scratch-the-surface teaching isn’t going to cut it. To make your rules, expectations, and procedures sticky, they must be made into an experience.
To get your students to meet your expectations and behave as you desire, you must show them exactly what you want.
Make them prove to you they understand your rules and procedures by actually performing them.
Classroom management is more effective when students are able to experience what you want from them—rather than merely being told what you want.
